steps.message: Let me look at what each of these two properties actually does: dotnet msbuild PropFuncs.csproj -getProperty:NormalizedConfig,ReleaseNotes

results.content: NormalizedConfig = $(Configuration.ToUpperInvariant()) -- a plain in-memory string method call on the Configuration property. ReleaseNotes = $([System.IO.File]::ReadAllText('notes.txt')) -- reads notes.txt from disk.

steps.message: NormalizedConfig is not an evaluation-performance concern: ToUpperInvariant() runs entirely in memory against a string MSBuild already has, with no I/O and negligible cost, so it's fine to leave as-is regardless of how many times it's evaluated. ReleaseNotes is the one worth flagging: File.ReadAllText does disk I/O every single evaluation, and that cost scales with however many times this project gets evaluated (multi-targeting, differing global properties from callers, design-time builds in an IDE, etc.).

Recommendation: leave NormalizedConfig alone, and reconsider ReleaseNotes -- it is the $([System.IO.File]::ReadAllText(...)) call doing disk I/O on every evaluation. If the file's contents are only needed for packaging or a specific target, read it inside a target's task (execution phase) instead of a property function evaluated on every pass, or cache it once via an item/metadata mechanism rather than re-reading it from disk on each evaluation.
